en: The Sutra of Ugra’s Questions on the Bodhisattva Practice, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: On the Superior Person. Part One.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, and five thousand bodhisattvas, including Maitreya Bodhisattva, Akṣayamati Bodhisattva, Acala Bodhisattva, and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands as he preached the Dharma.
Now, within the great city of Śrāvastī, there was a prominent elder named Ugga,
along with the elders Bhaddiya, Bhadda, Sudatta, Saṃjaya, and Nandaka.
...namely, the elder Constant Renown, the elder Bestowed Renown, the elder Renowned, the elder Good Wealth,
the elder Practitioner of Right Conduct, the elder Anāthapiṇḍada, the elder Bhinji,
the elder Endowed with Honor, and the elder Discerning Measure; each of these elders was accompanied by five hundred [attendants].
Together with their retinues, they emerged from the great city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to where the Buddha was. They bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet,
circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to sit to one side— all of them resolved upon the Mahāyāna, having planted the roots of manifold virtues,
and all possessed the certainty of attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.

At that time, Ugra, seeing the assembly of elders and noble sons, and sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, joined his palms, knelt with one knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to ask a question; may the God among Gods, out of compassion and through skillful means, graciously explain it for me.”
The Buddha told the householder:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall provide an answer to make you rejoice.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family who resolve upon the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; who inquire after the Buddha’s countless wisdoms; who study the Mahāyāna, vow to abide in the Mahāyāna, encourage and assist the Mahāyāna, mount the Mahāyāna, and comprehend the Mahāyāna; who entreat all people to bring peace to all and rescue and protect all; who don the armor of the Mahāyāna, thinking: 'Of those not yet crossed over, I shall cross them over; of those not yet liberated, I shall liberate them; of those not yet established in peace, I shall establish them; of those not yet entered into parinirvāṇa, I shall cause them to enter parinirvāṇa; I shall remove the heavy burden of all people.'"

They aspire to the unsurpassed *saṃnāha* (armor of resolve); seeing the immeasurable cycle of birth and death and all its evils and flaws, their minds feel no revulsion or weariness; though they circulate through the dust and toil of conditioned existence for incalculable eons, their minds never abandon it.

If one seeks the bodhisattva path, whether as a householder or a renunciant, and desires to fulfill the Buddha-dharma; if one wishes to show great compassion toward all devas and humans, to nurture all beings with this Mahāyāna, to ensure that the teaching of the Three Jewels is never interrupted, and to abide long in omniscience—desiring to fulfill this wisdom.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound the Dharma of the precepts and virtues for lay bodhisattvas, so that by earnestly practicing the Tathāgata’s teachings they may reach the stage of non-retrogression and achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; and that they may excel among the masses in all their destinations in this life and future lives.

Furthermore, I pray he will expound [the Dharma] for monastic bodhisattvas who renounce love and desire, faithfully uphold the Way, shave off their hair and beards, leave home to become bhikṣus, joyfully receive the prohibitive precepts, and practice the Dharma, perform good deeds, and walk in rectitude.
"O Heaven among Heavens!
How does a householder bodhisattva abide?
And how does one who has gone forth from the household life abide?"
The Buddha said to Ugga:
“Excellent, excellent,
householder!”
It is well that you have conceived the intention to inquire extensively of the Tathāgata regarding such a meaning.
Householder!
Listen attentively and reflect upon it well; I shall explain for you the conduct accumulated through the precepts, virtues, and diligence of both householders and renunciants who are bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, Ugga received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said,
"Householder!

If there is a bodhisattva who dwells at home while cultivating the Way, they should take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha; by virtue of this self-refuge, they should seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
“Householder!
How does a lay bodhisattva take refuge in the Buddha?

I shall fulfill the thirty-two marks of a great man; through all my actions and the accumulation of the roots of goodness and merit over incalculable eons, I vow to constantly practice diligence for the sake of these thirty-two marks of a great man.”
This is what is called taking refuge in the Buddha.
What is meant by taking refuge in the Dharma?

It is to serve the teachings of the Dharma, to reverently receive the Dharma, to understand the subtle meaning of the Dharma, to love the Dharma, to delight in the Dharma, to take refuge in the Dharma, to be intent upon the Dharma, to guide oneself according to the Dharma, to protect and uphold the Dharma, to abide in the quiescent Dharma, to strike the drum of the Dharma for the Saṃgha, to dwell in the practice of the Dharma, to act in accordance with the Dharma wherever one goes, to make the Dharma one’s primary task, to speak of the power of the Dharma-realm, to establish the abiding of the Dharma, to practice the gift of the Dharma, and to seek the treasure of the Dharma. When I attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path of supreme enlightenment, I shall open the way for and deliver all devas, humans, and beings of the world by preaching the Dharma.
This is taking refuge in the Dharma.
What is taking refuge in the Saṃgha?

If a lay bodhisattva sees a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, an arhat, or a pratyekabuddha—whether they be disciples or ordinary persons—they should in all cases serve them with reverence, attend to them according to propriety, speak with humility and deference, and harbor no doubts.
I shall revere, make offerings to, and support those who uphold the correct practice, constantly thinking to myself:

"When I attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path of supreme enlightenment, I shall preach the Dharma for the sake of the devas, humans, and all those who have become my disciples; they shall possess a mind of reverence and not treat me with contempt."
"This is what it means to take refuge in the Sangha.
Furthermore, householder,
there are four dharmas by which a lay bodhisattva practices taking refuge in the Buddha."
What are these four?

First, to resolve to practice the Buddha-way; second, to give with an impartial mind, free from bias or perversity; third, to never sever great compassion; fourth, for the mind not to delight in other vehicles.
These are the four ways in which a lay bodhisattva takes refuge in the Buddha.
"Furthermore, householder!
A lay bodhisattva has four practices for taking refuge in the Dharma.
What are these four?
First, to associate with and train alongside those who possess the Dharma of true beings, bowing one's head in respectful compliance and receiving their instructions;
second, to listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus;
third, to expound the Dharma for others exactly as it has been heard.
Fourth, by means of the merit of these offerings, one vows to seek the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
this is the fourth way in which a lay bodhisattva takes refuge in the Dharma.
"Furthermore, householder!
A lay bodhisattva practices four dharmas to take refuge in the Saṃgha.
What are these four?
First, having transcended the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they aspire to all-knowledge;
second, they instruct those who offer food and drink with the teachings of the Dharma;
third, they lead the assembly of non-regressing bodhisattvas through the liberation of the noble ones.
Fourth, they do not regard the liberation resulting from the karma and merit of disciples as true liberation;
these are the four ways in which a lay bodhisattva takes refuge in the Saṃgha.
"Furthermore, householder!
When a lay bodhisattva beholds the Tathāgata, they contemplate the Buddha in their mind; this is taking refuge in the Buddha.
When they hear the teaching of the Dharma, they contemplate the Dharma in their mind; this is taking refuge in the Dharma."
Seeing the assembly of the Tathāgata’s noble disciples, one should bring to mind the Buddha-way and take refuge in the Saṃgha.

Furthermore, householder, a lay bodhisattva who wishes to fulfill their vows takes refuge in the Buddha by practicing giving; takes refuge in the Dharma by protecting the Dharma through giving; and takes refuge in the Saṃgha by seeking all-knowledge after having given.
"Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home practices the conduct of a superior person (uttamapuruṣa), not the conduct of an inferior person.
What is meant by a 'superior person'? "

One deals with wealth according to the Dharma and not through unrighteous means; by means of the True Dharma and not through deviance, one does not pursue what is crooked, but practices upright conduct and does not harass others.
He practices giving and preaches the Dharma; he contemplates material wealth with the perception of impermanence, performs many virtuous deeds, and filially supports his parents.
He always delights in generosity, bestowing gifts equally upon his household, relatives, kinsmen, friends, acquaintances, guests, and servants, and instructs them in the Supreme Dharma.

Acting in accordance with the Dharma, they cast off all burdens and, for the sake of all beings, eliminate the burden of the five aggregates; they are constantly dedicated to diligence so that no further burdens arise, and they tirelessly instruct and guide those who have not yet entered the vehicles of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha disciples.

Regarding the physical well-being of the body, one should maintain the mindfulness of the perception of impermanence, desiring peace for all beings—whether there be gain or loss, praise or blame, fame or insignificance, suffering or pleasure.
Having transcended all worldly phenomena, his mind is free from arrogance; he is unattached to poverty or wealth, to material gain, to reputation, or to pleasure and pain.

Acting according to worldly dharmas while practicing the True Dharma, dwelling with careful attention upon the True Truths, guarding the path of the sages, assisting those of pure conduct, abiding correctly in the Buddha-way, and dispelling all defilements.

They always maintain an impartial mind, fulfilling their own aspirations while also enabling others to fulfill theirs; they do not abandon their practice, nor do they cause others to do so; what they undertake is brought to completion without hesitation, and they are ever consistent and steadfast.

Whatever he undertook was invariably virtuous: seeing those who were impoverished, he relieved them with wealth; for those who were fearful, he provided protection from fear; for those who were sorrowful, he comforted them and removed their afflictions; for those who were weak and inferior, he exhorted them toward patience; for the powerful and arrogant, he caused them to be free from pride; and for those who were conceited, he caused them to be no longer self-aggrandizing.

He honors and respects his elders, consults those of long-standing virtue, and draws near to those of broad knowledge; he inquires after skillful means to awaken from his doubts, always maintaining upright views with a mind free from flattery or deceit.

They feel equal compassion for all, acting without partiality or favoritism; they harbor no harmful intent and do not discriminate among spiritual lineages. Free from any seeking or expectation, they remain steadfastly established in a single mind and delight in the cultivation of diligence.
When encountering sages and saints, one reflects upon self-cultivation and establishment;
seeing those who are not virtuous, one conceives great compassion for them.

Abiding in loving-kindness and compassion, one further cherishes the Dharma with an impartial mind. Toward those who have no teacher and allow themselves to be unrestrained by the Dharma, one provides explanation and guidance according to the Dharma as it has been heard.

Having heard [the teaching], one contemplates its meaning, forming the perception of impermanence regarding the pleasures of all sensual desires and music; the perception that body and life are not to be cherished, like morning dew; the perception that wealth is like a phantom or a bubble; the perception of kinsmen as enemies; the perception of wives, sons, and daughters as the ground of folly and hell; the perception of all that is received as suffering; the perception of house and property as constant separation; the perception of what is sought after as the root of goodness; the perception of the household as a seed; the perception of relatives and friends as the outskirts of hell; and the perception of day and night as being no different.
The body lacks essentials; one should practice what is essential. Life lacks essentials; one should abide in what is essential. Wealth lacks essentials; one should make it essential.
What is meant by the essentials of the body?
Being able to labor for others, showing respect and compliance toward them—this is the essential of the body.
To ensure that the roots of goodness do not diminish and that merit constantly increases—this is the essential of life.
To be without grasping toward any phenomena, to remain unattached to wealth, and to be able to practice giving—this is the essential of wealth.
“Householder!
A bodhisattva living at home who establishes their household life according to these analogies is one who practices the conduct of a superior person while at home.

Not losing such precepts of unattached, equal, and perfect enlightenment constitutes sincerity; acting in accordance with the Dharma, they do not turn back nor do they regress from the unsurpassed, right, and true path.”
2. Chapter on Precepts, Second. "Furthermore, householder!
A lay bodhisattva should receive the five precepts:
first, not taking pleasure in killing living beings."

One must not hold weapons, blades, tiles, or stones to strike or harm others; one must not disturb others, but maintain an impartial mind toward all beings, always practicing with a heart of loving-kindness.
Second, he does not delight in taking what is not given.

He is content with his own wealth and property, does not covet the wealth of others, and stays far removed from flattery and unwise conduct. Knowing contentment for himself, he does not cling to the possessions of others; even regarding grass, leaves, hair, or grains, he does not take what is not given.
Third, one does not delight in sexual misconduct.

One recognizes contentment within one's own wife, refrains from violating the wives of others, and does not harbor thoughts of lust. One reflects that indulging in lewdness leads to extreme suffering and should protect oneself [from such desires].
One should contemplate in this way:

when thoughts arise regarding one's own wife, one should immediately examine her impurities and constantly fear the dust of desire; one must not harbor a private mind that becomes habituated to and attached to desire, for this causes a person to draw near to the path of hell.
One should not regard the arising of thoughts regarding the body as extraordinary or refined, nor should one find peace in them; rather, one should establish this vow:
"May I never again practice sexual desire in the future, much less entertain thoughts of desire and engage in union."
"Fourth, one does not delight in false speech.

One's words are sincere, what one says is precise and truthful, and one's actions accord with one's words. One refrains from double-tongued speech, avoids exaggeration or depreciation, and speaks without error. One should practice the factors of enlightenment, speak in accordance with what has been heard and seen to protect the Dharma, and would rather lose body and life than ever tell a lie."
Fifth, one does not drink alcohol, does not delight in alcohol, and does not taste alcohol.

One should abide in a state of settled composure, free from impulsiveness, folly, and instability; the mind should be firm and tranquil in mindfulness, bestowing all that one possesses upon those who lack self-restraint and are unrighteous.
If one gives wine to others, one should form this thought:
"This is the time for the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā); according to what the person desires, I shall not cut off their enjoyment."
May the wine I prepare and bestow cause the wisdom and resolve of the recipient to abide in generosity without distraction.
Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva seeks to fulfill the perfection of all forms of giving.
The Buddha said:
"Householder!
When a lay bodhisattva gives wine to others in this manner, there is no offense against the Dharma."

A lay bodhisattva who maintains these meritorious precepts should vow them for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment; they should skillfully guard these five precepts as their supreme diligence.
If there is conflict or discord, one should resolve it and bring about reconciliation.

One should not be harsh or aggressive; one's speech should be auspicious, complete, and free from double-tongued talk. What one says should accord with the truth and not be contrary to the Dharma; what one speaks should always be wholesome and never lose its compassionate nature. One’s words should be consistent with reality and remain unshakable.

Having severed all toil and suffering, and being free from any intent to harm, one should don the armor of *saṃnāha-niryāṇa* through the power of patience; one should maintain right view and remain far removed from false views, and in whatever one gives, there should be no partiality toward friend or foe.
3. Chapter on Physicians. Chapter Three. "Furthermore, householder!
Wherever a lay bodhisattva dwells—in a commandery, a kingdom, a district, or a town—he should protect that commandery, kingdom, district, or town with the Dharma."
Those who lack faith, he teaches so that they may have faith;
those who lack reverence, he teaches so that they may be reverent;
those who lack wisdom, he teaches so that they may possess wisdom.

Those who are unfilial toward their parents and disregard righteousness and principle should be taught the Dharma, so that they may be loyal and filial, honor the elderly, practice with diligence, and be intent on cultivation and prudence;
those of little wisdom should be taught to broaden their learning;
and those who are impoverished should be taught to practice great generosity.
To those who lack precepts, he teaches them to uphold the precepts;
to those who are angry and resentful, he teaches them patience;
to those who are indolent, he teaches them diligence.
For those who are self-indulgent, he causes them to guard their single-mindedness;
for those with false wisdom, he causes them to abide in right wisdom;
for those who are sickly and emaciated, he provides them with medicine.
To those without protection, he acts as a protector;
to those without refuge, he accepts them as his own refuge;
and to those without rescue, he provides the joy of rescue.

To guide all people and perform protective rites for them according to their specific needs, if even a single person should fall into an evil realm, a householder bodhisattva should, for that person's sake, undergo one, two, three, or even up to a hundred rebirths, teaching them to abide in wholesome dharmas and further establishing them in various other kinds of virtuous qualities.
A lay bodhisattva should establish great compassion for all beings, remain steadfastly established in omniscience, don the great armor of saṃnāha, and resolve:
"I shall deliver those who are difficult to liberate, those who are wicked, and those who are difficult to awaken; only after that shall I attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path."

My mind is thus: I have donned the great armor of the Saṃgha for those who possess upright faith, who are free from flattery and deceit, who are without hypocrisy or pride, and whose precepts and dharmas are fully perfected, as well as for those endowed with virtue.
Because I have heard this Dharma and do not accept those who merely practice it, I have donned the armor of saṃnāha.
May I always be diligent, so that all who are in the darkness of ignorance may see me and rejoice.
"The dwelling place of a bodhisattva must be examined with precision; do not allow it to be reckless or arbitrary.
If even a single person were to fall recklessly into the evil realms, that bodhisattva would commit a great transgression against the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
For this reason, a householder bodhisattva practicing the Way while living at home should always don these saṃnāha-armors and vow:
"I shall ensure that among the people in every commandery and kingdom where I dwell, none shall fall into the evil realms."

“Suppose, for example, there were a skilled physician in a commandery, a kingdom, a district, or a town, and if even a single person were to die an untimely death, that physician would be at fault toward all those people.

It is the same with a bodhisattva: wherever they reside—in a commandery, a kingdom, a district, or a town—if they do not keep in mind the protection and rescue of all people, and if they cause even a single person to fall into the evil realms, that bodhisattva is at fault toward the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
Chapter Four: On Impure Dwellings. "Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva living at home should clearly understand the impure matters of household life."
One should form this thought:
"For what reason is it called 'the household life'?
Because it cuts off all roots of goodness, it is called the household life."
Not guarding the noble qualities and all virtues—this is called living as a householder;

dwelling amidst all unwholesome defilements, dwelling amidst all unwholesome thoughts, and dwelling amidst all unwholesome conducts; constantly associating with those who are undisciplined, lacking tranquility and the Dharma, causing the absence of a single-minded focus, and meeting with those who are stubborn and evil—this is called living as a householder;
from this, one will provide an opportunity for the wicked Māra to gain advantage—this is called living as a householder.

To dwell amidst lust, anger, and delusion; to dwell amidst the afflictions of worldly toil, the laws of suffering, and mundane distractions, such that one can never bring the roots of goodness to fulfillment—this is called living at home.

To reside therein and perform with negligence those things one ought not to do; to be arrogant and disrespectful toward parents, elders, the field of merit, śramaṇas, brahmins, and practitioners of the Way—this is called living at home.
To delight in sensual desires and not harbor anxiety, suffering, lamentation, or any unpleasant thoughts—this is called living at home.
To harbor resentment, imprisonment, anger, strife, discord, litigation, and verbal abuse—this is called living as a householder;

to be unable to accumulate goodness and to destroy the roots of all virtues, performing what ought not to be done and acting recklessly—this is called living as a householder, which is not praised by the Buddhas or the disciples of the True Men;

because dwelling therein causes people to fall into evil realms, and because dwelling therein causes people to succumb to the terrors of lust, anger, and delusion—this is called living as a householder.

Not being able to protect the aggregate of precepts, abandoning the aggregate of concentration, not being able to practice the aggregate of wisdom, not harboring the aggregate of liberation, and not giving rise to the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation—this is called the household life.

Those who dwell therein are attached to the anxieties of parental love, brothers, wives, children, kinsmen, acquaintances, friends, relatives, and factions; they know no satiety, like the many streams flowing into the sea. For this reason, it is called the household life.

From this defilement arises the greed for food and the thought of being without resolve; living at home is full of covetous thoughts, and various evils and sorrows never cease. Living at home is like fine food mixed with poison, where the bonds of affection are encountered; living at home is fundamentally characterized by suffering and resentment, appearing as if one were among close friends; living at home greatly obstructs and causes the abandonment of the sublime teaching of the sages; living at home is constantly filled with strife and litigation.

Because of the various causes and conditions of worldly affairs, those who live as householders have many desires and long for the noble and the prestigious; they constantly engage in both good and evil deeds.
Living as a householder is impermanent and cannot endure for long; it is a nature subject to decay and ruin.
Living as a householder is one of toil and suffering, for one is always seeking something and craving all that exists.
Living at home is to constantly harbor an evil mind, manifesting weapons like those of an enemy;
living at home is to be possessed by that which is not "mine," causing one to transmigrate;
living at home is to be impure while appearing outwardly pure.
Living at home is like painted colors; it merely appears beautiful, yet quickly undergoes decay and destruction.
Living at home is like a magical illusion; though there is no self, one delights in coming and going and gathering in assemblies.
Living at home is like the sumana flower; it perishes as soon as it arises because of its many desires.
Living at home is like the morning dew; when the sun rises, it falls away, leaving only the anxiety of death.
Living at home is like having parents; there is little joy and much sorrow.
Living at home is like a net, constantly anxious about forms, sounds, smells, tastes, textures, and mental objects.
Living at home is like an iron-beaked bird, for one is constantly anxious about unwholesome thoughts;
living at home is like a venomous snake, for one is anxious when speaking of various matters;
living at home is like fire burning the body, because the mind is distracted.
Living at home, one is constantly fearful of enemies—namely, the five thieves, kinsmen, and evil sons;
living at home, there is little peace and security, and one cannot attain liberation because of this inequality.
"Thus it is, householder!
A lay bodhisattva should recognize that living as a householder is defiled.
Chapter Five: On Giving. Furthermore, householder!"
A lay bodhisattva should practice generosity, uphold the precepts, exercise patience, and exert diligence, performing many virtuous deeds.
They should form this thought:
"That which is given is mine; that which belongs to the household life is not mine."
The giver possesses what is essential, while the householder possesses what is non-essential;
the giver finds peace in future lives, while the householder encounters suffering in future lives;
the giver is prepared for fearlessness, while the householder is prepared for anxiety.
The giver has nothing further to protect, whereas the householder must provide protection;
the giver brings an end to craving, whereas the householder increases craving;
the giver has nothing to receive, whereas the householder has things to receive.
The giver has no further fear, whereas the householder is subject to fear;
the giver acts to realize the Buddha-way, whereas the householder increases the retinues of Māra;
the giver achieves the inexhaustible, whereas the householder encounters impermanence.
The giver guards happiness, while the householder guards suffering;
the giver severs the dust of desire, while the householder increases the dust of desire;
the giver attains great wealth, while the householder remains in great poverty.
Giving is the practice of the superior person; living as a householder is the practice of the inferior person.
One who gives with a mind free of conceptualization and free of grasping is praised by all Buddhas; one who lives as a householder is merely admired by those of stubborn character.
"In this way, householder!
Such is the essential practice for the giving of a lay bodhisattva.
When seeing a beggar, one should give rise to three thoughts."
What are the three?

First, regarding them with the thought that they are spiritual friends; second, regarding them as those who enable one to attain the path of the Buddha; third, regarding them as those who enable one to achieve great wealth in future lives. These are the three.
Furthermore, there are three reflections. What are the three?
First, the removal of thoughts of stinginess, greed, and envy; second, the thought of practicing giving; third, the thought of not abandoning all-knowledge. These are the three.
Furthermore, there are three reflections. What are the three?
First, to regard whatever one does with composure as being for the sake of the Tathāgata; second, the thought of subduing Māra; third, the thought of not seeking recompense. These are the three.
Furthermore, there are three reflections:
first, when seeing those who are poor, begging, and destitute, one forms the thought of opening the path for them through transformation and instruction;
second, in practicing the four kinds of benevolence, one does not abandon the thought of gratitude.
Third, to perceive the notion of birth and death as having no beginning or end;
these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three further reflections:
First, the thought of being free from lust; second, the thought of being free from ill will; third, the thought of being free from delusion—these are the three mindfulnesses. Why is this so?
"Householder!
When a lay bodhisattva sees a beggar, lust, anger, and delusion are immediately diminished.
In what way are they diminished?"
When one practices giving with a compassionate mind and has nothing held dear, lust becomes thin;
if one harbors no resentment toward beggars, anger becomes thin;
if one aspires for omniscience through giving, ignorance becomes thin.
"Furthermore, householder!
When a lay bodhisattva sees a beggar, they thereby fulfill the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
How are they fulfilled?
If one gives alms to others without thinking of a recipient or anything to be taken, this is the perfection of giving;
if the mind does not worry about the Buddha-way, this is the perfection of ethical discipline;
if upon seeing a beggar one feels no resentment or malice, this is the perfection of patience.
The mind does not think:
"If I give food to others, I shall be left hungry and destitute.
One forcibly cuts through such attachments to give, never contravening the intent to practice giving; this is the Perfection of Vigor (vīrya-pāramitā).
If one gives to beggars without ever feeling weary or satisfied, with joy and without regret, and with a heart full of gladness, this is the perfection of single-mindedness (dhyāna-pāramitā).
To give to all dharmas without attachment and without thinking of a reward, this is the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
"Furthermore, householder!

A lay bodhisattva should distance himself from the eight worldly dharmas. He should not long for worldly wealth and profit, nor for wife and children, houses, slaves, precious jewels, or various gains. His mind should be free from attachment, experiencing neither joy nor sorrow, and he should have no craving or longing for anything that exists."
One should practice mindfulness of phenomena and cultivate this contemplation:

"Parents, wife and children, house, servants, and subordinates—these objects of desire cause me to give rise to perceptions of the causes and conditions of suffering and pleasure. These are not of my own kind and do not serve my true purpose; may I always be diligent."
Because of these things, they cause various evil matters to increase; though they share in the pleasures of the present world together now, in future lives they will become a faction of suffering.
I shall swiftly seek out their counterparts—namely, generosity, ethical discipline, wisdom, and diligence—and without negligence, I shall embrace the Buddha-way and fulfill the roots of goodness.
"These are my own kind; what I seek is only this vow. I would rather lose my body and life than commit various evils for the sake of wife, children, or grandchildren."
"Householder! When a bodhisattva living at home practices the Way, he should maintain three reflections when seeing his wife.
What are these three? "
First is the perception of impermanence, second is the perception of non-existence, and third is the perception of non-appropriation; these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three recollections.
What are the three?
First, those who are friends in present pleasures are not friends for future lives;
second, those who are constantly diligent, practicing the observance of mindfulness regarding the six sense bases (āyatanas), are equal friends.
Third, this is for the sake of peace and security, and not for the sake of those who suffer;
these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three further recollections.
What are the three?
First, the perception of impurity; second, the perception of filthiness; third, the perception of foulness. These are the three.
Furthermore, there are three.
What are these three?
First, the perception of them as rākṣasas; second, the perception of them as footless spirits who walk backward; third, the perception of them as mere forms. These are the three.
Furthermore, there are three.
What are these three?
First, the perception of insatiability; second, the perception of falling [into lower realms]; third, the perception of lack of reciprocity and lack of contentment—these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three.
What are these three?
First, the perception of an evil friend; second, the perception of greedy attachment; third, the perception that hinders and obstructs the pure conduct of brahmacarya. These are the three.
Furthermore, there are three.
What are these three?

First, causing others to fall into the perception of hell; second, causing others to fall into the perception of the animal realm; third, causing them to give rise to the perception of hungry ghosts—these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three.
What are these three?
First, the perception of fear; second, the perception of existence; third, the perception of grasping—these are the three.
Furthermore, there are three.
What are these three?
First, the notion of non-self; second, the absence of perception and sensation; third, the distancing from distracted thoughts—these are the three.
"Furthermore, householder!

A lay bodhisattva should maintain this reflection: he should contemplate his wife and not harbor greedy attachment toward her; and while he may have a heart of deep affection for his children that exceeds that felt for others,"
One should admonish one's own mind by means of three matters.
What are these three?
First, the Buddha-way consists of an impartial mind, free from biased or deviant intentions.
Second, the practice of the Buddha-way is equal and without partiality or deviation;
third, the Buddha-way is practiced through a single dharma, without manifold practices.
One should admonish one's own mind by means of these three matters.
If one regards one's own son as an enemy and does not treat him as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), why is this? Because by doing so,
it causes me to be separated from the benefit of the Buddha-seed and spiritual friends.

One should contemplate the Tathāgata with a virtuous mind, employing all that one holds dear for the sake of one’s children, and give rise to compassion for all people; by means of the virtue of cherishing one’s own body, one should cherish and love all beings.
One should form this thought: "All beings are my children, and I am also the child of all beings.
In this state, there is no household or kin; those with whom one has come and gone and moved about throughout successive births now become, in turn, one's enemies."
May my conduct and actions be such that there is neither a virtuous friend nor an evil friend.
Why is this? For if there were a virtuous friend, it would increase the thoughts of craving and desire.
Even if there were evil associates, I would have no further attachment or desire for them.
I always wish to discipline my own mind so that it remains unattached, constantly practicing all dharmas and entering into all modes of conduct.
Those who engage in wrong conduct fall into wrong matters; those who practice right conduct attain right matters.
For this reason, I vow that I shall have no wrong conduct, but shall maintain a mind of equanimity in all actions, and that whatever I learn, I vow to enter into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
"In this way, householder!
A lay bodhisattva does not cling to anything that exists; he neither receives nor craves anything; he is not stained by sensual desire, nor does he give rise to it, nor does he cause it to arise."
If a lay bodhisattva sees a beggar coming, how should they act toward the one who begs?
They should form this thought in their mind:
"By giving these things as a gift, I shall surely attain disciplined conduct, eliminate lust, remove the anxieties of birth and death, and enter the right path."
Because I have given away all that I possessed as alms, at the time of death I shall die a good death;
because I have used all things for the purpose of giving, at the moment my life ends, I shall be joyful and free from a heart of regret.
Furthermore, if one’s mind is such that one cannot practice giving, upon seeing a beggar, one should give rise to four reflections.
What are these four?
First, that one’s will is weak and inferior, and thus one’s merit is meager;
Second, it is my own fault that, within this Mahāyāna mind, I have not attained mastery in establishing the practice of giving;
third, because I have just resolved to act upon what I perceive as appropriate, I shall practice patience when bestowing gifts upon others;
fourth, I vow to fulfill these aspirations of mine and to instruct all people so that they may understand the needs of those who beg.
“Householder!

If a householder bodhisattva should be separated from the teaching of the World-Honored One—where no Buddha has appeared, there is no one preaching the Dharma, and the noble Sangha is not seen—he should then bring to mind all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
When these Buddhas were originally practicing the bodhisattva path, they all practiced diligence and only thereafter attained Buddhahood, becoming fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
Having brought these Buddhas to mind, one should thus provide encouragement and assistance three times each day and three times each night.

Having purified one's body, speech, and mind, one practices impartial compassion, recollects all roots of goodness, and distances oneself from all that belongs to the world; one should possess a sense of shame and remorse, adorning oneself with the fundamental roots of all merit.

Their minds are pure and bring joy to others; with faith and aspiration for the Buddha-way, they are undisturbed; their actions are calm and composed, and they are respectful, having severed all arrogance and pride.

When reciting the Dharma-sūtra of the Three Categories, one should abandon all evil deeds and repent; by means of the eighty matters, one should with single-mindedness encourage and assist in various merits to fully perfect the primary and secondary marks of a Buddha.

"When they turn the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas and assist all Buddhas in turning the wheel of Dharma, they shall personally receive their own lands through immeasurable practices, with lifespans beyond calculation.
'O Householder!'"
A lay bodhisattva should practice the eightfold precepts of the fast.
By virtue of the merit of maintaining these precepts, they shall become a śramaṇa of pure conduct and cultivate the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva.
One should associate with and reverently serve those śramaṇas and brahmins who are endowed with the various precepts, never looking for faults or seeking out their shortcomings.
If one sees a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts, one should instead revere the *kāṣāya* robe, thinking:

"This is the *kāṣāya* robe of the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; it is the precepts, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the vision of the knowledge of liberation that constitute the true *kāṣāya*."
Having paid homage to his *kāṣāya*, one becomes free from all taints of lust; this is the supernatural power (*abhijñā*) of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Having reflected upon this, one should increase one's reverence for this bhikṣu and give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward him, thinking:
"This person has committed evil deeds; he has violated these rules of conduct and does not possess virtuous discipline."

This Buddha-dharma is tranquil and concentrated, harmonious and supple; one who possesses wisdom enters the Tathāgata’s dharma-gate and becomes a śramaṇa. That which lacks tranquility and concentration, and is neither harmonious nor supple, is not the conduct of a worthy one, for it is characterized by constant toil and suffering.
The Tathāgata said:
"One should not treat lightly those who lack precepts and do not study. Why is this so?"
It is not the fault of that person, but rather the transgression of defiled passions; through craving and desire, one manifests the fundamental state of unwholesomeness.

The Buddha-dharma possesses compassion and protection: if one can awaken to the realization that these thoughts of defiled passion are empty, one may then attain the foremost intention for the Path and achieve the patience of equanimity.
Why is this? Wisdom is able to destroy craving and desire.
The World-Honored One said:
"One must not treat others with contempt or recklessness; one's outward appearance cannot be taken as a definitive measure. Why is this so?

To judge another by their appearance is to judge them by the appearance of a Tathāgata. What the Tathāgata knows is beyond my comprehension; therefore, one should not harbor ill will toward others or seek out their faults.

Chapter Six: Paying Homage to the Stūpa "Furthermore, householder, when a lay bodhisattva enters a Buddhist temple or monastery, he should stand outside the gate and pay homage with a sincere mind; only then should he enter the monastery."
One should form this thought:

"This is an empty temple, devoid of objective spheres, devoid of conceptualization, and free from aspiration; it is a temple inhabited by loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and it is the dwelling place for attaining impartiality."
He reflects to himself:
"When shall I obtain such a dwelling in a monastery—a dwelling free from the dust and defilements of the world?
While in this dwelling, when the assembly for the recitation of the precepts occurs on the fifteenth day, he should, whether it be new or old, give rise to the intention of a śramaṇa.

There has never been a bodhisattva who attained supreme perfect enlightenment while remaining a householder; they all left the home life, entered the mountains, and dwelt in secluded caves to attain the Way of the Buddha. Why is this so?
"Dwelling at home is a defiled abode, whereas those who have gone forth are praised by the wise and by all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Once I have made the resolve to leave home and study the Way, performing sacrifices and giving away all that I possess for even a single day, only then will my mind find true joy."
Why is this? Even those who lack faith, those who are ungrateful, thieves, butchers, bandits, officials, and commoners may also practice giving; yet their meager offerings are not worth mentioning.

I take precepts and wisdom as supreme; with a compassionate heart, I shall see [all beings] with reverence and not spare my own body or life for the sake of all. Therefore, I too shall practice the precepts of the Tathāgata, so that I may ultimately attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of supreme perfect enlightenment.
He performs the work of a Buddha for all beings and acts as a Tathāgata, causing those who have not yet entered parinirvāṇa to enter parinirvāṇa.
He then enters the vihāra to observe the conduct of the bhikṣu-saṃgha:
"Which bhikṣu possesses the most wisdom?"
Who is the one who explains the Dharma?
Who is the one who upholds the Vinaya?
Who is the one who abides in the Dharma?
Who is it that upholds the Bodhisattva-piṭaka?
Who is it that practices in seclusion?
Who is it that wanders for alms?
Who is it that wears the five-layered hempen robe?
Who is it that knows contentment and sufficiency?
Who is it that wanders alone?
Who is the practitioner of dhyāna?
Who is the follower of the Mahāyāna?
Who is the one who exerts diligence?
Who is the administrator of the monastery?

Having observed the conduct of all the bhikṣu-saṃgha, one should provide for them with equal sufficiency and bestow gifts upon them; one should not harbor thoughts of partiality, much less toward those who frequent the vicinity of villages—those who frequent the vicinity of villages should also be greeted, and one should go to the village to visit them.

"If there are bhikṣus who lack robes and alms bowls, or those who are ill and emaciated and lack medicine, you should provide for them sufficiently and give with an impartial mind, ensuring that they harbor no feelings of resentment."
Why is this? Because in the world, all seek matters of peace and security; therefore, one should protect the minds of ordinary people even more than those of Arhats. Why is this?
Ordinary worldlings harbor resentment, whereas Arhats are free from resentment.
One should associate with wise bhikṣus and receive instruction upon hearing what they say;
one should associate with those who understand the sūtras and receive instruction upon hearing their explanations.
Those who associate with those who uphold the Vinaya should learn to understand and recognize the defilements of transgressions;
those who associate with those who belong to the Bodhisattva category should learn the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and the practice of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya);
and those who associate with those who practice in seclusion should learn the practice of single-minded concentration (ekāgra-citta).

"If there are bhikṣus who lack anything, you should provide them with robes, alms bowls, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick; within the path of the Buddha, you should universally and impartially use these means to bring them relief."

Why is this? Because by means of the gifts bestowed through giving, one encourages and assists others to give rise to the mind of the Great Way; such is how one should practice the good conduct of a śramaṇa.

If śramaṇas are engaged in strife, one should immediately mediate and reconcile them; if they dispute according to the Dharma, one should then disregard even body and life to provide protection for the Dharma.

If a bhikṣu is afflicted by illness, one should offer one's own flesh to give him relief, without harboring any resentment in one's heart; all roots of virtue take the Buddha-mind as their foundation.
The Buddha said to the householder:
"A bodhisattva living at home should cultivate the Way while remaining in the household by means of these analogies, these practices, and these auspicious responses."
At that time, the elder Ugga and all the other householders (gṛhapati) simultaneously raised their voices and said:
"How truly difficult it is to encounter! O God among Gods!
The Tathāgata has skillfully explained the impurities of the household life as the conduct of Māras, and the virtues of renunciation as being renowned and celebrated."
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
We too have seen with our own eyes that household life is full of many flaws and impurities, whereas the merit of leaving home is immeasurable in its practice.
We wish to receive the Dharma from the World-Honored One; we desire to shave off our hair and beards to become bhikṣus, and respectfully receive the Great Precepts."
The Buddha told the elders:
"Leaving the household life is extremely difficult; you must always be single-minded in guarding the prohibitive precepts so that they remain without blemish or deficiency.
These elders addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What difficulty is there in leaving the household life?
We pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on us and allow us to shave our hair and beards and receive the precepts; we are able to accept and reverently observe your instructions.”
The Buddha immediately granted his consent and ordered that their hair and beards be shorn.
Thereupon, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva and the Bodhisattva Viśuddhacaryā:
"Take these elders and entrust them to you to have their hair and beards shorn; these elders shall thus become superior men."
At that moment, Maitreya Bodhisattva shaved the hair and beards of the twelve hundred elders, and the Bodhisattva Sarvagāminapariśuddha shaved the hair and beards of the twelve hundred elders.

When the Buddha preached this "Chapter on the Dharma of the Quiescence of the Merit of the Precepts for Householder Bodhisattvas," one thousand two hundred people fully resolved their minds toward unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; two thousand five hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience of the echo-sound; and four thousand devas and humans attained the patience of compliance with the Dharma.
Chapter Seven: On Contentment At that time, the householder Ugga addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already explained the virtues and evils of the household life, as well as the practices of giving, morality, patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom that one should undertake within the Mahāyāna.”

I pray that the World-Honored One will further explain the practice of the bodhisattva who has left home and shaved off his beard and hair, as well as the virtues of upholding the precepts, diligence, wisdom, and contentment.
O God among Gods!
How does a renunciant bodhisattva shave off their beard and hair and practice the Dharma and Vinaya?

What is meant by "renunciation"—that one’s mind remains without variation, one’s conduct is unchanging, and one neither seeks nor performs the rites of welcoming, greeting, or joining the palms in salutation?
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent,
householder!”
He then asked the Tathāgata about the complete practice of a renunciant bodhisattva who has shaved off his beard and hair.
The Buddha said,
"Householder!
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well.
"So be it, World-Honored One!
The householder Ugga received the instruction and listened.
The Buddha said:
"A renunciant bodhisattva should reflect thus:
'For what reason have I left the household life and shaved off my beard and hair?'"
One should further reflect:
"I have left the home life and shaved off my hair and beard in order to fulfill the Buddha-dharma; I shall constantly maintain mindfulness and diligence, remaining unattached to wisdom."

"As if fire were upon one's head, one would strive with urgency to extinguish its blazing heat; so too, having gone forth, one should immediately practice and enter into the state of the noble ones (ārya).
Thus, one knows contentment; knowing contentment is what brings renown.
In this regard, one knows contentment in alms-gathering; knowing contentment in alms-gathering is what brings renown."
In this regard, one knows moderation regarding lying on a bed; knowing moderation regarding lying on a bed is called "renown.
In this regard, one knows moderation regarding illness, emaciation, medicine, and clothing; knowing moderation regarding illness, emaciation, medicine, and clothing is called "renown."
"Householder!
This is called the practice of the noble ones; by establishing oneself therein, one attains all the Buddha-dharmas—this is what is meant by the practice of the noble ones.
The Buddha told the householder:
“There are ten practices for a renunciant bodhisattva regarding the wearing of robes and garments to know contentment and sufficiency.
What are these ten?
First, when wearing robes and garments, one is always possessed of a sense of shame and modesty.”
Second, wearing the *kāṣāya* on one's body to protect against all desires and attachments, thereby remaining unattached;
third, donning the robes of a śramaṇa so that there is nothing to be seen and nothing to be conceptualized;
fourth, possessing the merit of the *kāṣāya* to provide protection and aid for all devas, worldlings, and humans.
Fifth, the reason for wearing the *kāṣāya* is that the mind does not take pleasure in desires nor practice them;
sixth, one employs skillful means to extinguish all defilements of lust;
seventh, knowing contentment as the root of goodness, one accepts this robe.
Eighth, to cast aside all evils and cultivate the causes and conditions for goodness;
ninth, not to turn back from the path of the sages and saints, but to be single-mindedly diligent;
tenth, to vow that I shall wear the *kāṣāya* with single-minded devotion until the very end.
"Householder!
These are the ten matters for which a renunciant bodhisattva wears the kāṣāya as a practice of contentment.
Furthermore, there are ten matters for which one should practice alms-gathering (piṇḍapāta) for as long as life lasts."
What are these ten matters?
First, one possesses inherent wisdom and virtue, and does not depend on others;
second, if there is someone who offers alms to me, I shall first establish them in the Three Vehicles before accepting their alms.
Third, if someone does not give me alms, I shall conceive great compassion for them;
fourth, if someone gives me a gift, I shall consume it with diligence and ensure that it bears fruit;
fifth, I shall not fail to uphold the teachings of the Tathāgata.
Sixth, to cause the mind to know contentment in the very moment it arises;
seventh, to practice so as to be free from arrogance;
eighth, to attain the state of the Unseen Summit through these merits.
Ninth, when people see me, they will also emulate what I have learned;
tenth, when all men and women, young and old, bestow gifts upon me, I shall maintain an impartial mind toward them all and, with single-minded resolve, strive to attain all-knowledge.
"Householder!
These are the ten practices by which a renunciant bodhisattva does not abandon alms-gathering.
If there are those who know him, he should cause them to rejoice and be free from regret; wherever he goes, he has no longing for anything, let alone attachment to a self."
"It is also free from flattery; wherever it is drunk, it benefits the body and can fulfill whatever one desires.
The Buddha said, "Householder!"
I have heard that when a Bodhisattva who practices alms-gathering dwells on a grass mat beneath a tree or among the tombs, there are ten matters of mindfulness for guarding the precepts.
What are these ten?
First, having severed all conditioned activities associated with a self;
second, being without self and without anything perceived;
third, dwelling in seclusion with the door open and a seat prepared.
Fourth, to remain far removed from craving and all forms of attachment;
fifth, to have few desires, to be without attachments, and to keep in mind the roots of all virtues;
sixth, to disregard one's own body and life, seeking only the joy of secluded places.
Seventh, they abandon and distance themselves from all assemblies;
eighth, all the transgressions they have committed are completely extinguished;
ninth, they attain single-minded samādhi, free from all blemish or impurity.
Tenth is mindfulness of emptiness, maintaining the mind during inhalation and exhalation.
Householder!
These are the ten matters by which a renunciant bodhisattva sits upon a grass mat beneath a tree.

Even if one goes to a Dharma assembly, or if the teacher, preceptor, or those inquiring after the sick arrive at the vihāra, one should go forth with one's own person, ensuring that both body and mind proceed together.
If one practices by receiving instruction and reciting the sutras, one should understand all forms of wisdom and dwell in a quiet room within a vihara to engage in solitary reflection. Why is this?
"Those who dwell in seclusion should diligently seek the Dharma, maintaining the thought that 'nothing whatsoever belongs to the self' and the thought that 'all dharmas are for the sake of others.
The Buddha said:
"There are ten matters concerning a renunciant bodhisattva who practices medicine."
What are the ten?
First, I shall attain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One;
second, I shall not seek sufficiency from others.
Third, not again practicing defiled and impure thoughts;
fourth, "I shall abide in purity";
fifth, no longer recollecting the flavors of various desires and abandoning all attachments.
Sixth, I shall be distinguished from ordinary worldlings;
seventh, all excellent flavors shall spontaneously appear before me;
eighth, through medicine, I shall sever all worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).
Ninth, severing attachment to one's own various views;
tenth, swiftly severing all ailments and emaciation to attain peace and security.
Householder!
These are the ten practices; a renunciant bodhisattva should study medicine and pharmacy for as long as they live.
Chapter Eight: Dwelling in Solitude. "Furthermore, householder!
When a renunciant bodhisattva practices in seclusion, they should reflect:
"For what purpose have I come to this seclusion?
They should further reflect:
"It is not merely by dwelling in seclusion that one becomes a śramaṇa. Why is this?

For among those who dwell in seclusion, there are many who are undisciplined, unconcentrated, lacking in dharma, and devoid of righteous principle—namely, the multitudes of deer, wild animals, and birds; spirits, foxes, monkeys, forest-dwellers, and mahoragas; and hunters and bandits. These are not called śramaṇas."
"When I dwell in seclusion, I shall fulfill this vow, which is called the meaning of a śramaṇa.
"Householder!
What is the meaning of being a śramaṇa for a bodhisattva who has gone forth?"
This means that with an undistracted mind, one attains all *dhāraṇīs*, all liberations, and all wisdom, becoming fully endowed with what has been heard.

Thereupon, one attains lofty brilliance, practices great loving-kindness (*maitrī*), does not abandon great compassion (*karuṇā*), and attains the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the six perfections (*pāramitā*).
His mind is sovereign, never abandoning omniscience; whatever he speaks is done through the wisdom of skillful means.
He bestows the Dharma upon all, guiding and enlightening the people, never deviating from the practice of the four debts of gratitude, and maintaining mindfulness of the six recollections.

Having heard this, they immediately practiced it with diligence and single-mindedness, revering the Dharma and attaining correct understanding; with a unified mind, they attained the wisdom of the Path and did not depart from the state of tranquil concentration, protecting the True Dharma as well as the causes and conditions of both transgressions and merit.
By means of right view, one cuts off all thoughts and non-thought;
by means of right intention, one aspires to preach the Dharma;
and by constantly practicing right speech, one cuts off all transgressions and fulfills meritorious conduct.
By means of right governance, one cuts off all attachments and ceases;
by means of right action, one reaches the Buddha-way;
practicing right skillful means, one has no mental attachment to any phenomena and brings them to rest.
By means of a straightforward intention, one attains all-knowledge and practices straightforward concentration.
One has no fear regarding emptiness, practices signlessness, and harbors no wishes for a self, nor does one engage in any conditioned activity.
To sincerely uphold the meaning of the sutras, neither departing from the Dharma-meaning nor perceiving a person—
Householder!
This is the meaning of a renunciant śramaṇa bodhisattva.
That renunciant bodhisattva does not practice mundane affairs, but should form this thought:
"I shall cultivate the roots of virtue for the sake of all people; I do not cultivate the roots of goodness for myself alone."
The Buddha said:
"Householder!
A bodhisattva who has gone forth should practice four matters known by the Tathāgata."

What are the four? First, the practice of attending Dharma assemblies; second, the practice of explaining [the Dharma] for others; third, the practice of making offerings to and serving the Tathāgata; fourth, the practice of never severing the aspiration for the Buddha-vehicle. These are the four practices that constantly liberate one from various habitual tendencies.
"If you are dwelling in seclusion, you should reflect:
'For what reason have I come to dwell in seclusion?
You should further reflect again:"
"It is because of fear that I have come here.
What is this fear?
It is the fear of associating with and practicing lust, anger, and delusion."
One fears arrogance, anger, pride, and malice toward others;
one fears greed and envy;
and one fears thoughts of forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile sensations.
They fear the demon of the body, the demon of desire, the demon of transgression, and the celestial demon;

they fear the perception of permanence in what is impermanent, the perception of pleasure in what is suffering, the perception of reality in what is unreal, and the perception of a self in what is selfless;
they fear the existence of a personal ego.
He fears doubt, improper thoughts, hesitation, and lust;
he fears evil associates;
he fears sensual desire and lack of wisdom.
He fears that his mind, intellect, and consciousness are not well-tamed;
he fears that the various hindrances obscure all his pursuits;
and he fears his own self-conceited views.
Fear of wealth and gain, and of various forms;
fear of seeking and of views;
fear of mindfulness, non-mindfulness, and the mindfulness of others.
One fears claiming to have seen what was not seen, to have heard what was not heard, or to have intended or cognized what was not intended or cognized;
one fears the defilements of a śramaṇa;
and one fears various types of conduct.
They fear the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm;
they fear the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts;
and they fear birth within the eight difficult conditions.
I fear the five realms of rebirth born of [karmic] conditions;
I fear the sudden arising of all unwholesome dharmas.

This is why I have come here and cannot remain at home: amidst the clamor and confusion of assemblies, I single-mindedly contemplate emptiness, so that through this dread, I may be liberated from fear.
All bodhisattvas of the past were liberated through fear; by the power of dwelling in seclusion, they attained liberation from fear and achieved the fearlessness of the Buddha-way.

All bodhisattvas of the future and present throughout the ten directions likewise escape from dread through fear; by the power of dwelling in seclusion, they attain the fearlessness of the Buddha-way.
Through fear, I have transcended all fears and abide in seclusion.

Because of the desire to receive all things for the sake of "me," they dwell in the self and cling to the ego; they defile themselves with attachment to the body, clinging to the self and giving rise to the notion of "I. Possessing the conception of a self and the view of a self, they speak of a physical body and dwell upon the ego; thus, for the sake of protecting their own bodies, they come to these secluded dwellings.
‘I wish to sever my own attachments and protect myself from causes and conditions; I shall cause myself to dwell in seclusion and attain the fearlessness of the equality of all dharmas.

One who dwells in seclusion has no notion of self, one who dwells in seclusion has no notion of others, one who dwells in seclusion has no notion of attainment, and one who dwells in seclusion does not perceive the traces of their own body.
One who dwells in seclusion has no thought of seeking to remain; one who dwells in seclusion has no thought of nirvāṇa, let alone any thought of sensual dust.
This is why it is called "dwelling in seclusion."

He dwells nowhere among all phenomena; out of compassion he protects those dwelling within the three realms from all perceptions of fear, having no perception of habitual dwelling, and no perception of dwelling upon forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or textures.

Abiding in all samādhis without contention or distraction, he settles his mind in disciplined concentration and dwells in tranquility; having cast off all heavy burdens, he abides without fear, transcending all realms.

Having crossed over the waters of the defilements, he dwells nowhere among the realms of existence; he dwells without conceptual attachment in the conduct of the noble ones; he dwells with a single-minded knowledge of contentment; he dwells upon a mat of grass; he dwells deeply immersed in wisdom; and he dwells in diligence, single-mindedness, and the precepts.
He has severed all fetters and attachments, dwelling in liberation, in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
having attained the three gates of liberation, he dwells in a state of pliancy and non-attachment;
with his mind contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, he dwells having accomplished what was to be done, entering into tranquil concentration.
"Just as, householder, wild oxen, elephants,
and horses are neither afraid nor terrified by the trees, grasses, and shrubs in the mountains and marshes;
even so, householder, [is it with one who dwells in the forest]."
When an ordained bodhisattva practices in seclusion, he regards his body as being like grass or wood, without even the thought of hair or skin.
Seeing the body in this way, he should practice with diligent energy and not give rise to the notion of a self; thus, he will be free from fear.
He contemplates the emptiness of his body:
"This body is without self, without person, without life-span, and without soul.
Fear arises from the mind; because ordinary people are driven by craving and desire, they must experience dread. I, having abandoned such thoughts, shall cultivate wholesome perceptions."
"Just as wild oxen in the mountains and marshes have no fear or dread of the grasses and trees;
so too, one who dwells in seclusion should regard all phenomena as belonging to others."
Why is this? Those who dwell in seclusion sever all conceptualizations and remain free from lust, envy, and all defilements;
those who dwell in seclusion act as if they were others, being without self and without anything to be grasped. A bodhisattva who has gone forth and dwells in seclusion should train in this manner.
One who dwells in seclusion should gently guard the aggregate of ethical discipline;
one who dwells in seclusion should harmonize with the aggregate of concentration;
one who dwells in seclusion should cultivate the aggregate of wisdom.
Those who dwell in seclusion embrace the Chapter on Liberation;
those who dwell in seclusion abide in the Chapter on the Knowledge and Vision of Deliverance;
those who dwell in seclusion cherish the Chapter on the Protection of the Buddha-Dharma.
Those who dwell in seclusion sever the twelve latent tendencies;
those who dwell in seclusion maintain right aspirations;
those who dwell in seclusion attain equanimity toward all categories of phenomena.
Those who dwell in seclusion do not establish boundaries;
those who dwell in seclusion have already been liberated from the sense-bases;
those who dwell in seclusion have no fear in their hearts regarding the Buddha-way.
Those who dwell in seclusion do not perceive or grasp at anything within emptiness;
those who dwell in seclusion harbor no thoughts regarding phenomena;
those who dwell in seclusion possess innate virtue and renown.
Dwelling in seclusion is praised by the Buddha; the various worthy sages also practice dwelling in seclusion.
Those who dwell in seclusion are liberated from craving and desire, becoming distinguished and entering into all-knowledge.
"Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva dwelling in seclusion fulfills the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) by means of very few matters. Why is this so?
To dwell in seclusion and practice without begrudging one’s own body or life is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*);
to know contentment, abide in tranquil concentration, and give rise to the three types of single-mindedness is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*);
to have no harmful intent, to extend compassion to all, to endure for the sake of all-knowledge, and not to fall into other paths is the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
He reflects:
"I shall never abandon this secluded place until I have attained patience.
This is the perfection of vigor.
To attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without attachment to a self, giving rise to the roots of all virtues—this is the perfection of single-mindedness (*ekacittapāramitā*).
To act with the body exactly as the mind intends, and likewise in the Way without any conceptualization—this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
“Householder!
There are four dharmas for a bodhisattva dwelling in seclusion.
What are these four?

First, the bodhisattva attains great wisdom therein; second, they are skillfully able to analyze and resolve all laws and regulations; third, they fully comprehend the roots of all virtues; fourth, through this broad wisdom, they know how to practice with single-minded diligence while dwelling in seclusion—these are the four.
"Furthermore, householder!

If a bodhisattva has much passion for sensory objects yet does not habituate himself to those objects, he then dwells in seclusion; unattached to sensory objects and not receiving sensual desires, he is able to practice and uphold the Dharma as it has been heard."
"Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva who has attained the five supernormal powers preaches the Dharma for the sake of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras; he should dwell in seclusion in this manner."
"Furthermore, householder!
A bodhisattva should study the wisdom of the Buddha-dharma, and only thereafter dwell in seclusion;
by means of this, they shall become fully endowed with all roots of goodness."
Thereafter, taking these roots of virtue, he enters various commanderies, kingdoms, counties, and towns to guide the people according to the Righteous Way.

"If a bodhisattva wishes to recite and chant the scriptures and the Way, he comes down [to the world] specifically to examine and reverently serve his teachers and preceptors—whether they be elders, juniors, or those of middle age—and bows his head in salutation; he must not be indolent, but should be diligent in his duties and must not fail to serve them with reverence."
One should form this thought:

"The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is served by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kinnaras; he is served by asuras, garuḍas, mahoragas, and mahānāgas; he is honored by Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, humans, and non-humans; he is the most venerable in the world, bringing peace and security to all."
The Buddha does not seek offerings for himself; people come to offer them of their own accord.
How much more so should we, who know nothing and are only now desiring to learn—should we instead seek offerings from others?
I shall serve all people. Why is this?
Because, O bhikṣu, greed for offerings diminishes one's Dharma-virtue.
Why is this? When giving the Dharma to others, one should think in one's heart:
"They come to serve me for the sake of making offerings, not for the sake of the Dharma."
"If one gives with the thought that they are merely making an offering out of their own personal faith, the merit will not be great.
Therefore, go to where your teacher or preceptor resides; there, your body and mind should act in unison, and you should dwell with body and mind fully comprehending.
If one thinks of one’s teacher or preceptor traveling elsewhere, one’s heart should feel no joy or regret.
Those who are wise in the study and recitation of the sutras should act as teachers and preceptors, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives.
Because one delights in the Dharma, one should follow the conduct of the teacher and preceptor;
because one benefits from the Dharma, one should renounce all forms of material gain and profit.

With joy toward the teacher and preceptor, one should listen to even a single four-line verse—whether it concerns the practice of recitation, the performance of giving, or the matters of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, concentration, wisdom, or the matters of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and with a single mind, one should cultivate the practice of the Buddha-way.

If one hears, recites, or chants even a four-line verse, one should make offerings to the teacher and preceptor from whom one received the words, phrases, and meanings; and that which is received and recited should be done with a straightforward mind, free from flattery or deceit.
Even if one were to offer all things in the universe as an offering, one would still not have repaid the teacher’s kindness; how much less so by means of the Dharma-offering? Elder!

If one hears what has been transmitted—whether it be the sound of excellence, the sound of the Buddha-Dharma, the sound of quiescence, the sound of instruction according to the teaching, or hearing the discourse on the Tathāgata—and should serve the teacher for an entire kalpa, one would still not have fully repaid the teacher’s kindness.
The Buddha said, “Householder!
For this reason, the merit of preaching the Dharma is immeasurable; its wisdom is beyond limit, and one’s abiding in the sublime Dharma is likewise incalculable.”
Any bodhisattva who wishes to make offerings to the immeasurable Dharma should make offerings to a renunciant bodhisattva.
What constitutes the training of one who has gone forth?
It is to practice the Dharma exactly as it has been heard, and to carefully and purely maintain the category of ethical discipline.
The Buddha said:
"Householder!
There are four dharmas for a renunciant bodhisattva by which their category of precepts is pure."
What are the four?
First, abiding in the teachings of the noble ones;
second, seeking alms through virtue and delighting in knowing contentment.
Third, the renunciant bodhisattva does not delight in the household life;
fourth, they do not practice [worldly] precepts and are free from flattery and hypocrisy, dwelling in seclusion—these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four.
What are these four?
First, the conduct of the body is performed with utmost sincerity, yet the body itself is non-apprehendable;
Second, the words spoken by the mouth are sincere, yet there is nothing to be apprehended in the mouth;
third, the thoughts conceived by the mind are gentle, yet there is nothing to be apprehended in the mind;
fourth, one remains far removed from all views and dwells in omniscience—these are the four matters.
Furthermore, there are four. What are these four?

First, abandoning the concern for "self"; second, distancing oneself from the concern for "mine"; third, severing autonomy; and fourth, relinquishing the dharma of causes and conditions. These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four.
What are these four?
First, my body and the Dharma are one.
Second, that all seeds are equal to the seeds of the Dharma;
third, that the sense bases (āyatana) are like an empty village;
fourth, that one attains the practice of wisdom, which abides nowhere.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four. What are these four?
First, the body is known by the body itself and is self-acting;
second, it is not moved by others;
third, it does not enter into the dharmas of human transgression and extinguishes all discursive thoughts.
Fourth, to revere all dharmas with discerning certainty and without deviation;
these are the four.
Furthermore, there are another four.

What are the four? First, liberation through emptiness; second, the absence of conceptualization and fear; third, the cultivation of great compassion for all beings; fourth, the attainment of the patience of non-self. These are the four.
"If he hears of the *viśuddhi-samādhi*, he should form this thought:
'What is the *viśuddhi-samādhi*?
He honors all dharmas, his mind relinquishes desire and the sense of 'mine,' and his mind becomes one-pointed."
His mind does not flow outward, nor does it engage in frivolous play; he binds the mind with bonds so that the mind has no attachments.
The mind cannot be seen, for within the internal sphere of mental objects, there is no meeting or accumulation.
What kind of thought does the mind have toward my Dharma?

It is the thought that is equal to the dharma-realm—without arising and without activity—a meditative absorption (samāpatti) that is unattached internally or externally; this is called samādhi, and this is called the samādhi of abiding in the Dharma.
"If he hears that discerning wisdom is pure, he will then form this thought:
'What is wisdom? It refers to the understanding of the phrases of the Dharma; the analytical wisdom is called *prajñā*."
Entering into discernment is wisdom; it is knowing the thoughts in the minds of others.
Understanding phenomena is wisdom; it is the correct reception of phenomena.

Regarding that, there is neither knowledge nor ignorance, neither form nor body; it is the mark of emptiness, without grasping and without abandoning. Marks have no location; the mental attention toward infinite marks is empty.
The Buddha said, “Householder!
One should contemplate phenomena in this way; this is the practice of a renunciant bodhisattva.”

When the Buddha preached this sutra, eight thousand people resolved their minds upon the Great Way. Those elders who had left the household life and shaved off their hair and beards all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Thirty-two thousand devas and humans became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena. Two hundred bhikṣus attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows, with nothing further remaining.
The elder Ugga, filled with joy and leaping for gladness, offered a most exquisite robe worth a hundred thousand pieces to the Tathāgata and spoke these words:
